canonical_definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is as a standardized, open-source evaluation framework, library, or software suite for running language-model benchmarks in a reproducible and comparable way. Most definitions describe a broad suite of downstream tasks, while some narrow it to zero-shot or few-shot settings, multiple-choice tasks, or text-only and short-context subsets, with examples such as ARC, BoolQ, HellaSwag, Wikitext, and LAMBADA. A smaller line of work presents it as the common protocol for leaderboard-style assessments or as a unified framework for evaluating generative language models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 11 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims span many targets rather than a single construct. Most commonly, papers use it to measure commonsense reasoning, general ability, reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and in-context learning. Across the behavioral-indicator links, the same broad pattern appears, with papers using it for capability evaluations such as zero-shot and downstream-task performance.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers use it as a common framework for benchmark suites, often reporting zero-shot or few-shot accuracy under default or recommended settings and, in some cases, averaging across 0-shot to 5-shot runs. It is used alongside 23 linked instruments, most often HellaSwag, MMLU, PIQA, WinoGrande, and GSM8K, and papers position it both for broad model comparisons and for validating specific task setups, including text-only, generation, and multilingual evaluations.

Concerns raised. One paper reports that the default setting "did not allow some models to complete their full chain-of-thought reasoning before being truncated," identifying truncation under the default configuration as a concern in that use case.

characterization_sections.label: What it is.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing framing is as a standardized, open-source evaluation framework, library, or software suite for running language-model benchmarks in a reproducible and comparable way. Most definitions describe a broad suite of downstream tasks, while some narrow it to zero-shot or few-shot settings, multiple-choice tasks, or text-only and short-context subsets, with examples such as ARC, BoolQ, HellaSwag, Wikitext, and LAMBADA. A smaller line of work presents it as the common protocol for leaderboard-style assessments or as a unified framework for evaluating generative language models.

characterization_sections.label: What it is claimed to measure.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link it to 11 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims span many targets rather than a single construct. Most commonly, papers use it to measure commonsense reasoning, general ability, reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and in-context learning. Across the behavioral-indicator links, the same broad pattern appears, with papers using it for capability evaluations such as zero-shot and downstream-task performance.

characterization_sections.label: Space of uses.
characterization_sections.text: Most commonly, papers use it as a common framework for benchmark suites, often reporting zero-shot or few-shot accuracy under default or recommended settings and, in some cases, averaging across 0-shot to 5-shot runs. It is used alongside 23 linked instruments, most often HellaSwag, MMLU, PIQA, WinoGrande, and GSM8K, and papers position it both for broad model comparisons and for validating specific task setups, including text-only, generation, and multilingual evaluations.

characterization_sections.label: Concerns raised.
characterization_sections.text: One paper reports that the default setting "did not allow some models to complete their full chain-of-thought reasoning before being truncated," identifying truncation under the default configuration as a concern in that use case.

characterization:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is as a standardized, open-source evaluation framework, library, or software suite for running language-model benchmarks in a reproducible and comparable way. Most definitions describe a broad suite of downstream tasks, while some narrow it to zero-shot or few-shot settings, multiple-choice tasks, or text-only and short-context subsets, with examples such as ARC, BoolQ, HellaSwag, Wikitext, and LAMBADA. A smaller line of work presents it as the common protocol for leaderboard-style assessments or as a unified framework for evaluating generative language models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 11 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims span many targets rather than a single construct. Most commonly, papers use it to measure commonsense reasoning, general ability, reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and in-context learning. Across the behavioral-indicator links, the same broad pattern appears, with papers using it for capability evaluations such as zero-shot and downstream-task performance.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers use it as a common framework for benchmark suites, often reporting zero-shot or few-shot accuracy under default or recommended settings and, in some cases, averaging across 0-shot to 5-shot runs. It is used alongside 23 linked instruments, most often HellaSwag, MMLU, PIQA, WinoGrande, and GSM8K, and papers position it both for broad model comparisons and for validating specific task setups, including text-only, generation, and multilingual evaluations.

Concerns raised. One paper reports that the default setting "did not allow some models to complete their full chain-of-thought reasoning before being truncated," identifying truncation under the default configuration as a concern in that use case.
